extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in film, satire, climate communication, media criticism, and progressive politics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for making and assessing feature-film satire about the climate crisis — how to balance comedy and tragedy, reach broad audiences, and make persuasive political/media critique that prompts real-world engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global playability / cross-cultural appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Can you do comedy that plays in Nigeria, Vietnam, Brazil, the States, India, Pakistan?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design jokes, situations, and emotional beats that translate across national and cultural contexts; aim for themes and character dynamics that resonate internationally rather than relying on narrowly local references. McKay cites Netflix as a distribution vehicle that enabled a 'world movie.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix of farce and dark tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Toggle between a broad farcical comedy and a really dark tragedy to reflect contemporary reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend genre tones so the film can be uproariously funny while still conveying the painful stakes of climate catastrophe. Use tonal contrast to underscore the absurdity and the human cost; avoid flattening everything into pure satire or pure melodrama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociological clarity about power and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use satire to explain how power works and why certain things happen — show the media, corporations, and the political system as mechanisms that impede collective action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the film as a piece of sociology: make institutional incentives, self-interest, and structural drivers legible to audiences rather than merely lampooning individuals. Scenes should reveal why institutions behave as they do (ad revenue, careerism, status).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize the issue over celebrity gossip
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus attention on the climate emergency and scientific evidence rather than personal drama or celebrity dirt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid narratives or marketing that let critics or outlets reduce the film to gossip about the filmmaker or cast; ensure interviews and publicity direct conversation back to the substantive crisis and data rather than personal scandals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity over aesthetic subtlety when truth is ridiculous
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t assume subtlety is always preferable — when the reality is absurd, a clearer, more pronounced satire can be necessary to pierce denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If institutional behavior is itself ridiculous, making the satire 'obvious' can be a virtue: the goal is to expose dynamics audiences are not seeing, not to hide the thesis behind artful ambiguity. Be aware critics may label this 'heavy-handed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict media gaslighting and institutional incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Show how news organizations, pundits, and journalists can gaslight the public or deprioritize existential threats because of economic and social incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete portrayals of advertising reliance, greenwashing, careerism, and editorial choices (burying climate stories) to reveal the mechanisms that keep the public uninformed or misled. Use recognizable analogues (parody morning shows/newspapers) to prompt audience recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make scientists and evidence visible
rubrics_metrics.description: Give scientists a clear voice and present actual data and scientific statements within the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict scientists being heard (or ignored) on mainstream platforms; present empirical claims credibly so the audience can connect fictional events to real-world science. Avoid sidelining the science in favor of pure rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spark curiosity and public conversation about the crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: The film should lead viewers to ask 'why aren’t we doing anything?' and to discuss the real-world crisis rather than only debating the film’s tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use storytelling and interviews to channel attention into policy, institutional critique, and civic questions. In publicity and afterword materials, encourage audiences to engage with the underlying issues rather than meta-critique of the film’s style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use emotion and disruptive tactics to persuade
rubrics_metrics.description: Disruptive protest and emotional appeals have been shown to sway people; neoliberal media structures are particularly vulnerable to emotional pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely solely on facts; craft emotionally powerful scenes and moments that motivate viewers. Consider depicting or endorsing disruptive tactics as one of the effective levers for change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic use of platform and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Reach matters: placing a film on a major global platform (e.g., Netflix) can massively amplify impact (hundreds of millions of viewers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose distribution channels that maximize exposure across countries and demographics. Coordinate marketing to ensure the film's themes are visible to diverse audiences and translated appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate portrayal of denial dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that denial can intensify even as evidence becomes more visible — public acknowledgement may decline as the problem becomes apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict the counterintuitive real-world phenomenon where increasing visibility of a crisis can lead to deeper entrenchment of denial; use narrative arcs that demonstrate escalation of misinformation, defensive identity behaviors, and collective rationalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose moral hazard and profit motives (e.g., geoengineering/mining solutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight how self-interest, profit incentives, and magical-solution narratives (geoengineering, mining the comet) derail meaningful action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrate how proposed technical fixes can be co-opted by private gain and how moral hazard operates; make the stakes of such schemes clear to audiences so they understand why they are politically attractive but dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance entertainment with substantive proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Be entertaining while also demonstrating that there are concrete things society could do (mobilization, carbon removal research, policy interventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid nihilism; present feasible policy or societal responses within the story or supplementary materials to keep alarm productive rather than paralyzing. Offer examples of large-scale mobilization analogies (World War II-style) and concrete research/policy paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft memorable, morally clarifying lines and choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Include clear moral pivots or memorable lines (e.g., 'sometimes you gotta just do the right thing') that crystallize the film’s ethical claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dialogue and character arcs to distill the film's normative center so audiences leave with an actionable moral takeaway, not just satire for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show both institutional failure and individual decency
rubrics_metrics.description: Portray a contrast between corrupt or complacent institutions and ordinary people or individuals who genuinely care — maintain 'faith in humanity' even while critiquing power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humanize activists, scientists, and ordinary citizens; avoid reducing everyone to caricature. This balance helps the film inspire action rather than hopelessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design publicity and media engagements to steer discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Use press tours and interviews to keep conversations focused on the crisis and scientific evidence rather than letting media narratives default to gossip or style wars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When promoting the film, prepare spokespeople and materials that repeatedly redirect questions to climate policy, data, and systemic critique. Be prepared for personal attacks and have a strategy to pivot back to substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and counter framing that dismisses alarm as 'doomer' rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid being sidelined by labels that paint alarmism as unserious or paralyzing; frame urgency as a rational, solution-oriented stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide context about actionable options and emphasize that alarm is based on empirical evidence and possible remedies; preempt talking points that delegitimize alarm by showing organized solution pathways.
